How I would build a Bangladesh supplier base.

Not one factory and a big first order. A staged model that proves quality, delivery and margin at each step.

1Map20–30 factories

Bras, briefs, bodies, nightwear, swimwear, lace and moulding.

2Screen10–15 suitable

Technical capability, capacity, compliance, quality and cost.

3Qualify5–8 qualified

Samples, assessments and cost benchmarking.

4PilotControlled orders

Small production runs with performance measured.

5Scale3–5 core + backups

Backups so no single factory is a risk.

I wouldn't build a large supplier network before proving the economics. Pilot first, measure quality, delivery and margin, then scale only where the numbers support it.

Small FOB gains move margin more than most people expect.

Margin is decided by pattern and consumption, construction time, lace and elastic, MOQ and factory allocation, long before a discount is asked for. I set a baseline, then a realistic target for each style, rather than promising a blanket saving.

Across 13 lingerie styles I analysed, margin ranged from 6% to 18%. The opportunity is understanding why, style by style.

Try it: the customer price is fixed, so slide the FOB.

If Bangladesh is right for you, this is how the first 90 days go.

I would present it as an approach to test, not a promise. Scale only after the pilot proves quality, commercial value and reliability.

Understand

Days 1 to 30

Review the portfolio, suppliers and baseline costs. Map Bangladesh factories and capabilities.

Develop

Days 31 to 60

Shortlist and qualify suppliers, benchmark costs and samples, negotiate and review compliance.

Pilot

Days 61 to 90

Run pilot orders, track quality, OTIF and actual against target FOB, and present the first supplier scorecard.

Year one: supplier intelligence, qualified suppliers, repeat business and margin work, then a scalable network with structured reporting. First goal, a commercially reliable Bangladesh. Regional sourcing only after that is proven.
